I advocated it long before the minister was in this House.

It was my hon.
friend's own party that passed the act. Why did they not put it in force? In the act as passed by the hon. gentleman's friends it was provided that before the law came into force it should be proclaimed by order in council. This shows that those responsible for the act knew what they were doing and that the time to make the law effective was a matter for discretion. I am sure the hon. gentleman will be glad to know that of the cheese graded in 1923, 77.08 graded No. 1. That was pretty good to start with. In 1924, showing the stimulus given by the grading system, 84.38 of the cheese graded No. 1. In 1925 the stimulus was still more apparent, because 85.60 graded No. 1. I should not be disputing with my hon. friend as to why the act was not enforced. Apparently in the first place there was doubt as to the desirability of [DOT] grading, and in the second place the effect the grading as introduced would have upon the quality was unknown.

Provision is made for a grant of So,000 to the National Dairy Council. I would ask the minister if he has had any representations _ as a result of the meeting of the National Dairy Council held in Quebec last fall or this winter with reference to the Australian treaty. As I understand it, the National Dairy Council is a sort of parent institution which fathers all the provincial dairy associations. Such being the case I think its representations should have due weight with the minister. My information is that the dairy council did make some representations finding a good deal of fault with the Australian treaty. A number of other dairy associations I believe, in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have also made representations along the same line. Furthermore, I should like to ask the minister a question in view of the fact that in the first three months of the present year no less than four million pounds of butter entered Canada from New Zealand and Australia. When he considers that in the whole of the calendar year 1925 less than 70,000 pounds came in, I would like to get his opinion as to what effect that is having on the dairy industry. I should also be glad if the minister would take this opportunity to give us his own idea as to just what the effect of the treaty has been, since it has been in force, and what will the general effect be upon the dairy industry.

The National Dairy Council is not very much enamoured of those provisions of the Australian treaty that reduced the duty on New Zealand and Australian butter by two cents and three cents respectively, and they have so expressed themselves. The dairy association of Canada have so expressed themselves, but the Mari-times have not expressed themselves one way or the other. Out on the prairies, where we do not look for very much agitation on behalf of protection, there developed quite an agitation against that phase of the Australian treaty. I had the pleasure of meeting members of the dairy council here in Ottawa after their meeting at Quebec city, and they made a very fair representation in regard to their case. I asked them if they did not think it would be fair, before pronouncing judgment, to give this system a year's trial to see how it would work out. That was a month ago. I think my hon. friend knows that if it never works out any worse than it has this year we would hope the treaty would remain in force forever so far as the effect on the dairy industry is concerned. Under the provisions of the treaty we have had the magnificent amount of three cheeses coming in. So far as cheese is concerned we can leave it out. I do not think any eggs have come in, so that we can leave that item out as well, too. With regard to butter, in spite of the fact that it is coming in under a two-cent tariff reduction from New Zealand and a three-cent tariff reduction except where the dumping clause is applied automatically, from Australia, ever since it started to come in the price of butter has persistently gone up, week after week and month after month, until it has reached the price of 47| cents retail, and has been sold to consumers in almost every market in Canada for over 50 cents a pound. I think the reason was that there was such an unusual shortage in Canada that it was not possible to get Australian or New Zealand butter rapidly enough to fill the vacuum or depress the prices. The result has been that the shortage continued all winter and prices kept stiffening up all the time. From 43i cents it went up to 47i cents to the retailer. That is the highest point it reached, and the price to the consumer was 52 cents. Consequently the price of butter has been so high that, in spite of the reduction in duty an agitation has sprung up for the restoration of oleomargarine as a substitute. That is no dream. The National Council of Women in this city about a week ago so expressed themselves. The price is beginning to come down, not because of the Australian or New

Supply-A griculture
Zealand butter coming in, because that is all here or is on the way here, but our natural production, which usually occurs about this time of the year, has been coming in, and the prices have been dropping until now they are about what they were at the beginning of January. The shortage of butter was so great that it could not be supplied quickly enough to keep the price from going up, and it went up steadily till about ten days ago.
I do not know that we can take this as a criterion as to how it will affect the trade another year. One thing is sure, that if we enter another winter with the same shortage and the same conditions we will have the same prices. There is not sufficient storage space at Vancouver to keep the butter and supply it quickly enough to take care of the vacuum. On the other hand, if we do not ship short then we will have sufficient butter ourselves, and there will be no attraction for New Zealand or Australian butter. Australian and New Zealand butter did not displace one pound of Canadian butter. It was not here. The farmers and dairymen had sold it under the attractive prices of last summer and had the money in their pockets, and we had to turn around and buy from Australia and New Zealand.

Does the
minister say we had no reserves of butter?

We had not so
many reserves. We had about 12,000,000 pounds less than the year before or 6.000,000 pounds less than the average of the last five years.
But we had several millions in reserve?

Yes, but we were
12,000,000 pounds short of the previous year's supply. That 12,000,000 pounds could not come across the Pacific in the four months, because there was not sufficient cold storage to take care of it. The Pacific route had storage room for 8,000,000 pounds and that left a shortage until our own production came and took care of it, and the prices went down. The prices will very soon be down to an export basis. All through the winter, while the Australian butter was coming here, it was ten cents above export prices. As long as our butter is selling ten cents higher than the world price there can be no very great grievance, and we should be willing to try this treaty out in a normal year, when we enter the winter with a normal supply on hand.

Four million pounds of butter from Australia and
New Zealand came in early this year, and the minister says that the price is the highest that it has been for many winters. That is probably true, but we must remember that it is the butter produced by the Australian and New Zealand farmers that is being sold at the high price. The Canadian farmer should be getting that price. I contend that when this legislation was put through in June of last year it discouraged the farmers, and they curtailed their production during last summer, in preparation for this winter's output, because they knew that in all prabability the Australian and New Zealand butter would come in. The Australian and New Zealand butter has come in. If our people had had their butter ready to sell at the high price, the Australian and New Zealand butter would have come in in any case, and they would not necessarily have got the high price which means so much profit to them. The Australian and New Zealand butter would have come in and would have been sold at a less price than the Canadian article, even if our butter had been on the market. I maintain it is the threat of that Australian and New Zealand butter coming in that is affecting the dairy industry and will continue to affect it. The minister also said that if the conditions so far were any criterion, he hoped the Australian and New Zealand treaty would continue forever. I do not think the dairy industry in this country will back him up in that statement. I think it has already given them a severe shock and the very threat of that product coming in when the price goes up is bound to have a deleterious effect on the industry.

As regards the production this year we have it as being forty per cent higher than that of last year. Even in the winter this year the production was greater than that of last winter, and as regards any production we have in the winter the farmers reap the benefit of the higher price.
Not for the 4,000,000 pounds that came in from Australia and New Zealand.

What else could we have done? The farmers could not produce butter by flashlight. There are ways of making artificial butter, but there is only one way of making the real thing and the real thing was not here to eat or to sell. I believe our supply or stock on hand fell short by about
12,000,000 pounds of what it was a year ago; that quantity was not in sight and people had either to eat their bread dry or to get butter from somewhere. We brought it in from the logical place where we could get the best
Supply-Agriculture

butter at the lowest price, and that was New Zealand and Australia. I am really astonished at people complaining that we got good butter at a cheaper price while at the same time our farmers were getting a higher price for butter than they had since the end of the war. Next year-and we expect to be here for several years yet-my hon. friend may have the argument on the statistics but we shall have to wait until that time. In the meantime all the figures are against my hon. friend's contention. The price on March 19 for first grade Australian butter at London prices converted into Canadian currency was equivalent to 36J cents.
That is the London price?
Yes.

What is the Vancouver price?
Mr. MOTHERWELL. The Montreal price the same day for first grade creamery butter in the wholesale jobbing houses was 47 cents, or eleven cents higher. I was giving it at ten cents higher.

What was it in 1923? The minister says that prices now are higher than they have been at any time since the war. I have his own circular letter, this campaign literature, showing the price in 1923. Will he just read from it?
I gave my copy to the leader of the opposition.
I will read it. The price of butter was as high as 52J cents.
That is retail.
This does not say retail. It gives the prices at Montreal in the month of February and these are his own figures. The high price is 521 cents, which is the highest price quoted in the whole list.
The price I state has been going up all winter.

The price that I have reference to is published in this campaign literature, under date of 1923, not this year at all, and yet the minister says that the price now is higher than it has been at any time since the war. That statement does not agree with his printed letter.
The hon. member is reading from the wrong scripture.

A few minutes ago the minister said that this treaty came into effect only in October and that no harm had

been done since then, although 4,000,000 pounds have come in. That sounds very much like the campaign literature that I am going to read from now.
That is Tory stuff.

No. Hon. members will recognize the photograph on the outside, that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). This piece of campaign literature is published in September last. Let me read this sentence:
No ill effects as yet have flowed from the Australian treaty.
This has the signature of the Liberal party and the photograph of the Prime Minister on it.
We always sign ours.

This says:
No ill effects as yet have flowed from the Australian treaty.
Ju^t imagine! This was dated in September and the Australian treaty came into effect on the first of October.

That is easily
accounted for. My hon. friend does not know the effect of his own campaign regarding this treaty. My hon. friends were howling about this for months before in anticipation of it, and as a matter of fact in Alberta and British Columbia, as a result of their propaganda against it, the dairymen dropped their prices even before the treaty came into effect. When my hon. friends opposite were in power there was no complaint about Australian butter coming in. I will give the total imports of butter from Australia and New Zealand for different years. In 1911, the last year that the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power, the total imports of butter from Australia amounted in round figures to 900,000 pounds. The very first year that my hon. friends were in power the total from Australasia amounted to 2,241,000 pounds, or nearly three times as much of what they call this villainous stuff came in. [DOT]
That is for a year. My hon. friend did better in four months.

My hon. friend
would apparently rather be eating oleomargarine which his leader wanted to impose upon this country, oleomargarine that is made from intestinal parts of animals and other things. In 1913 the jump is three times as great again; there was 6,116,000 pounds of this so-called bad stuff imported from Australasia.

Supply-Agriculture
Did we hear any Tories going around the country howling their heads o2 about that? We never heard a word about it. The people of Canada thought it was a good thing to be able to get first class butter at a low price from their sister dominion, and if it had not been for the election last fall they would have continued to think t'he same thing. But my hon. friends have such a propaganda factory at Toronto that they have persuaded the people it is a bad thing for them to buy this butter from their sister dominion at two cents less.
What was the duty at that time?

Four and three
cents. It has been that for a long time, for a quarter of a century. My hon. friend cannot divert me from giving these figures by telling us bed-time stories. In 1914, 6,959,000 pounds of this kind of dope came in from our sister dominion, or nearly twice as much as has come this year, and yet not a word was said about it. I would ask the hon. member for Lincoln what the people of this country would have done if they lacked 4,000,000 pounds of butter with which to lubricate their bread. I will wait for an answer. We entered upon the winter with a shortage of 12,000,000 pounds, and we all know that you cannot order butter from the cow overnight.

The minister is
certainly an expert at buffoonery. He knows that there were 10,000,000 pounds of butter in storage at the time this butter was brought in from Australia. What I would not have done was to take the duty off any of our own farm products.
That is no answer. The fact is that we had 6,000,000 pounds less than the average of the last five years.
And did 4,000,000 pounds that came in meet our needs? If it did, then I can tell the minister that we had several million pounds in storage.
We were short of butter or we would not have ordered any from abroad.
There is another matter I want to have answered.
I want this one settled first.

A few minutes ago the minister referred to the fact that there was an automatic dumping clause in effect on Australian butter. Has that dumping clause 14011-134
been enforced against one solitary pound of Australian or New Zealand butter that has come into Canada in the last three months?

The answer from
the department of the minister of Customs indicates that it has. The dumping clause was applied to Australian butter, as it is applied to all other butter.
I asked a plain question and the minister is not giving me a plain answer. I want to know whether one pound of Australian butter was subjected to the dumping clause.
It is all subject to the dumping clause, whether from Australia or elsewhere.
I understood the minister to say that this butter from Australia and New Zealand did not lower the price in Canada, but on the contrary almost stimulated it.
I did not say that.

Does the minister remember the telegrams read in this House from Vancouver and Victoria indicating that the first shipment of Australian butter had the effect of reducing our price by from two to four cents?

I did not say what effect it had; I was assuming for the sake of argument that it did lower the price. I believe that the people of Vancouver, as I know was the case in Alberta, hearing so much talk about great quantities of butter coming in from Australia, lowered the price before that butter ever landed on their shores. Vancouver would be the logical place where the greatest effect would be felt from an importation of Australian butter inasmuch as it is the frontier of the antipodes. I know further that the Alberta creamery men had an arrangement with the produce dealers of Vancouver to supply them with butter at two cents below what it was at the time the treaty went into effect, provided they would patronize the Alberta creameries. They lowered the price in anticipation.

The minister gave us to understand a while ago that there was such a shortage of butter in this country that we had either to allow Australian and New Zealand butter to come in or eat our bread unbuttered. Now he tells us that in anticipation of Australian and New Zealand butter coming in the price immediately dropped in Vancouver and elsewhere from

Supply-Agriculture

two to three cents per pound. On what? On the butter we did not have, for he said just now that we had no butter. According to his own statement we had a shortage. He tells us however that the price of our butter, which was non-existent, fell two, three or four cents per pound. The minister quoted figures in regard to importations covering a period going back eleven, twelve, thirteen and fourteen years, but he did not complete his statement Perhaps he has the figures before him. I have not all the facts in my mind, but my impression is that during those years we had a shortage. Notwithstanding the statement of the minister, however, as to the present shortage in this country, I think I am right in saying that we had an exportable surplus of butter last year of between twenty-five and thirty million pounds.

More than that;
34.000.	000 pounds.

Then what becomes of the minister's statement that the price went up because there was an absolute shortage here? The position which I take in this matter is this: there are two classes of people concerned in the sale of butter-the purchasers, whose representations have a right to be considered, and the consumers, who have an equal claim upon our consideration. That is the principle that should govern us in fixing the tariff, and I maintain that so long as Canada has an exportable surplus of
30.000.	000 pounds of butter that very fact in itself should be an absolute guarantee to the consumers that they would never have to pay more than they should for the article. That is reasonable. At the same time I hold that the producers of this commodity in our own country have the first claim on our own home market. Australia and New Zealand take that view in regard to their own products. They have a high duty on butter, because they have a large exportable surplus, and they have also a considerable tariff on meats. They are one of the largest meat exporting countries in the world, and they say that inasmuch as they have more butter and cheese and meat than they know what to do with, they do not want outsiders to send those commodities into their country. They guarantee to the farmers that only Australian and New Zealand butter, meat, eggs and cheese shall be used on Australian and New Zealand tables. That, I maintain, is the proper attitude for us to take here, especially in view of this fact, which should not be lost sight of, that the dairy interests cannot be considered only in relation to the summer months, but from the standpoint of

the entire year. In the course of the twelve months we have a severe winter during which the cost of production is necessarily high, and the producers of Alberta and other places in Canada where there exists a surplus of butter have a distinct grievance. At the very time in the winter months when the cost of production is at its highest in Canada, they are forced by the Australian treaty to compete with the product imported from that country, which is produced at a time when the cost of production is naturally low.
,It is all very well to theorize on the subject of free trade and other questions of that sort, but we must not lose sight of the practical element. We cannot afford to forget that climatic conditions in this country are different from those that obtain in Australia and New Zealand, and owing to that difference our farmers are compelled to invest large sums of money in specially adapted barns and stables, in silos and other equipment, and to spend a good deal in providing forage and storing it for the winter, keeping their stock during that trying season at a heavy expense. It is therefore unreasonable, it is eminently unjust to expect the farmers in a country like Canada to compete on even terms with Australian and New Zealand butter and similar products by allowing those products to come into this Dominion at a very low rate of duty, or nominally free. That is the position which I take and it is the position taken by dairymen generally throughout the country. I do not believe that there was any shortage of butter such as the minister speaks of. There might be a shortage in this or that locality, but that might happen at any time; but on the whole our trade figures show, as the minister himself has admitted, that Canada did not have a shortage of butter last year. On the contrary we had a large exportable surplus of some 30,000,000 pounds and as the minister says, even more than that. My contention is that we should so arrange the tariff as to guarantee to our Canadian farmers that their produce shall have first place on Canadian tables and not the produce of countries which have a distinct advantage over us by enjoying a milder climate.

There is not much in the moralizing of the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) to which I take exception, but he tried to make my statements appear self-contradictory. I admitted that butter-fat prices dropped in October, not only when the treaty came in but even a little before it did, owing to all the noise that was made by my hon. friends prior to the election. But the prices

Supply-Agriculture
went up again before the New Year as soon as it was understood that there was a shortage, and that condition continued until about two weeks ago. That is what I said, and there is nothing contradictory in it. As to our being short of butter, I did not say that; what I said was that we went into the winter with a shortage. It does not matter whether we exported 25,000,000 or 30,000,000 or 100,000,000 pounds of butter; the fact remains that so long as that butter went out of the country during the summer we did not have it in Canada. We could not sell our butter and have it at the same time. We therefore entered upon the winter with a shortage of
12,000,000 pounds as compared with last year, and that is what made butter prices go up. The great tide of Australian and New Zealand butter which had been dammed by the longshoremen's strike naturally flowed, when liberated, into the places where there was the greatest shortage, and one of those places happened to be Canada. Butter made right in this country had gone over to Great Britain, and when the shortage occurred here that butter was shipped back, paying a duty of four cents to enter the country of its origin.
Was that not due to the strike in Australia which prevented the Australian product from reaching the British market?

The Australian
butter was held back through the strike.

That was responsible
for the enhanced price.

Yes, because the
Australian butter could not get to the British market; there was a shortage there which attracted Canadian butter, so that When the winter came we had a shortage as compared with the previous year. We had therefore either to buy butter somewhere or go without it. My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) apparently would have preferred to have us go without it, and that is a matter of choice.

This minister
can argue in a circle about as well as anyone I ever came across. He says there was a shortage here of 12,000,000 pounds, and in a circular letter, written in his own office over his own signature, only a few days ago, he has this to say:
The present agitation originated largely with some dealers and creamery operators who hoped to realize higher prices on the stock of butter which they had on hand and for which the producers had been paid fall prices.
Tf you can beat that I want to hear the next one.
I can give explanations-

You bet you
can.
-but I can never guarantee that the hon. gentleman will understand them.
You won't yourself.

Of course there
were stocks on hand, but the fact that is of significance is that we had 12,000,000 pounds too little as compared with the year before. That is the point.
And 4,000,000 pounds we imported would save the situation?

Of course, where
would you have got it?

And we had
butter in storage. How much is in storage now?

Oh, what is the
use of talking?

There seems to be in the
examination of this question a doublebarrelled difficulty. The minister himself says that Australian butter coming in cost the consumers a higher price, and if I understood him correctly I think he said that the fear of this same influx of butter drove down prices in Canada. And if we are to believe the statement that has been made, the producers in the country, or at least a great many of them, went out of business reducing their stocks and herds, so that there was an adverse effect, in consequence, as regards the production of butter in Canada and the necessity for the consumers to pay higher prices. I think it is true that the dealers in butter in this country, sometimes in the summer, when there is usually a large quantity produced from an abundance of grass feed, later on keep up their prices anticipating a higher market. When therefore the treaty went into effect, or was about to go into effect, the dealers in Canada were on the verge of panic, and they sold heavily of their reserve stocks. The minister speaks of Tory propaganda, at the time of. the election, creating a hubbub in the country and frightening the dealers and producers; but there would have been no propaganda had there been no legislation of this kind proposed or any treaty in sight. There are therefore two evils in connection with this matter, one bearing harmfully upon the consumer, and the other affecting the producer.

One word more. I listened attentively to the minister and I heard him say that the price in Canada to-day was ten to eleven cents higher than the export price. Did I understand the minister correctly?
I read the dates.
That is all right, but approximately?

That is so, and that was
maintained for some considerable time?
Yes.

I wish to call the attention of the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. King) to that remark. Here is a statement by the minister admitting that the export price does not govern the home market price, the spread being 10 cents. I want hon. gentlemen to remember, therefore, that when they say the export price in the world market governs the price at home, it is at last on record, through the Minister of Agriculture, that that is not so.
When you have an exportable surplus.
We had an exportable surplus.
Not at the time the minister speaks of.

It is very peculiar, Mr. Chairman; I try to speak in a very mild manner, but the dogs of war hop on me from all comers of the House whenever I make a statement. It must be that I get under somebody's skin, and I can assure you that I do not mean to do so. I merely wish to point out what I hope is quite obvious to anyone giving a moment's thought to the subject. The minister says there is no exportable surplus, but in the next breath says there are
7.000.	000 pounds in storage, and we export
30.000.	000 to 40,000,000 pounds; we have . 7,000,000 pounds more than are normally required. That is an exportable surplus. If the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) cannot see that that is an exportable surplus, he should have a pair of glasses.
It does not follow that there is an exportable surplus because you have a small reserve stock on hand for your own use.

My hon. friend is like the man in some parts of our own country who, when laying in a little sauerkraut for the winter, puts in eleven barrels for his own use.

Seven million pounds is practically one quarter of our total export.

How much is
that for each person in Canada?

It is 7,000,000 pounds more than is normally consumed, if that is anything to my hon. friend. Of course it would be a little difficult for him, I fancy, to figure that out offhand, but he may be one of those lightning calculators who come from certain sections of the country, and able to figure these things out rapidly. But my point is that when we have hon. gentlemen here telling the country and this House that the home market price is governed by the export price, we now know once and for all, from an authoritative source-the Minister of Agriculture himself-that that is not always true.

I feel sorry for my hon. friend if he does not see the difference between what the hon. member
11 p.m. for Weyburn (Mr. Young) said and the conditions which have prevailed during the last four months. We were an importing country for the last four months; that is the reason.

With 7,000,000 pounds in
storage we are importing?

What is 7,000,000
pounds, spread over this Dominion?

It is a quarter of our
total exports.

I think perhaps
my hon. friend finds difficulty in understanding the situation. My hon. friends from Nova Scotia make good butter and export it, but Canada as a country has been an importer of butter during the past four or five months. That is what the howl has been about, because we have imported 4,500,000 pounds of butter.

Under a low
tariff.

That is what the
kick is about; hon. gentlemen seem to want to pay more. If the producers have suffered, and I do not admit that, it must be remembered that the consumer has benefited. They can take it whichever way they like.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt this question is agitating the rural parts of Canada very much. During the last election the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. King) had ^o write a letter to the Globe saying that he

Royal Assent
did not vote in favour of the Australian treaty. Someone inadvertently said that he had voted in favour of it, and he had to go on record to the contrary. That shows the feeling in his riding, when he had to correct that impression before he could hope for reelection. There is one last question I want to ask the minister. What in his opinion will be the effect on Canadian dairying of the recent increase in the American tariff on butter from eight cents to twelve cents?

We will be less apt to go there. There is very little butter goes there, it will go to the world market, which is the United Kingdom. Occasionally some goes to the United States but not very much, and that amount will decrease under the twelve cent duty.
Would there not be less if our tariff was higher?
They do not bring butter in here.

I
mean from other countries as well as from the United States. Would not the same principle hold?
As soon as we begin exporting, which will be in a month or so, there will be no butter coming from anywhere, because we will be exporting it.

I think we have had an
interesting discussion on this very important subject. It is now eleven o'clock and many of our agricultural members who would like to take part in this discussion are not here. I want to say a few words myself, and I think under the circumstances the minister might let this stand over until after Easter.
Very well.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if my hon.
friend offers no objection, perhaps we might pass this item, with the understanding that we will have a full discussion on it afterwards.
We will have the whole question of dairying up again on the live stock vote. I would like to make a little progress.

The minister has not forgotten that he made a similar promise once before and when he got into the estimates, where we could discuss the particular item, he called on the chairman to shut discussion off.
I did not make a promise.

The minister's memory is as poor as his dependability. That occasion is very dear in the minds of a number of us, and I do not think the minister could have forgotten it. It was on a similar vote. I am ready to accept any measure of repentance by the minister, and if he will promise not to do that again, so far as I am concerned I am prepared to let this go through.
I say I never did it and I never intend to do it.
If we produce the specific case, will the minister beg pardon?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He will recant.
Yes, he will recant.
He will crawfish.
I do not think he, is too old to reform, even yet.
No, we are always improving.

And with the distance the minister has to go, he can start any time. So far as I am concerned, I am willing to let the item go through, on condition that this discussion will come in at a future time.

Progress reported.
